title: The Third Eye Opens
hookLine: spring arrives on Shiva's mountain out of season, and Kama, the god of desire, takes aim at the god who is deep in meditation
carry: kama: an aim of life, never the master
tomorrow: how will Parvati win the god who burned desire?

cards: On a frozen mountainside, the snow starts to melt. Out of season, trees burst into flower. Bees show up, a cuckoo sings, the breeze turns warm and sweet.
Every living thing on the mountain feels it, except one. Under a tree, Shiva sits in meditation, perfectly still, eyes closed, as if spring were somebody else's business.
Behind a bush, with a bow made of sugarcane and arrows tipped with flowers, crouches Kama, the god of desire. He's been sent on a mission, and he's nervous.

teach.b: Here's why he's there. Since Sati gave up her body, Shiva has withdrawn into meditation.
Sati has been born again as Parvati, the daughter of the mountain king, and she comes every day to serve him: flowers, water, a clean place to sit. He doesn't look up.
Meanwhile a demon named Taraka has a boon, and in the Shiva Purana only a son of Shiva can defeat him.
So the gods need Shiva to marry, and Shiva is busy being still. Indra, king of the gods, sends Kama, and Spring with him. Kama waits for his moment, Parvati standing near, and lets an arrow fly.

Shiva's mind stirs; he opens his eyes and looks at Parvati. Then he catches himself, looks for the cause, and sees Kama with his bow. Fire bursts from Shiva's third eye, and Kama is burned to ash on the spot.
You met this at Holi, on day ninety-six; here is how the book tells it. Rati, Kama's wife, falls weeping beside the ashes, and she's promised her husband will live again.
Now, what Hindus take from it is not that desire is bad.

teach.h: KAMA: ONE OF LIFE'S FOUR AIMS.
teach.b: Kama, desire and pleasure, is one of the four purusharthas, the aims of a human life, alongside dharma, doing right, artha, making a living, and moksha, freedom.
But Shiva is the great yogi, and many read the third eye as the eye of wisdom: desire that tries to command him burns. And Kama doesn't vanish.
From then on he's called Ananga, the bodiless one, love moving everywhere unseen.

teach.h: AN AIM OF LIFE, NEVER THE MASTER.
teach.b: Whatever wins Shiva will have to come from Parvati herself. That closes a week full of fire.

how: Hindus tell the burning of Kama in the Shiva Purana and in poetry and dance; Shiva is often shown with a third eye on his forehead, and in some places the story is remembered at Holi or in spring festivals.

a book of spells for making someone fall in love

s: Kama's arrow had no effect on Shiva
for a moment Shiva's mind stirred and he looked at Parvati. then he saw Kama, and the third eye opened.
Parvati had come every day to serve Shiva in meditation
flowers, water, a clean place to sit, and he didn't look up.
in Hindu teaching, desire is simply evil
kama is one of the four aims of life, with dharma, artha and moksha. it belongs; it just doesn't rule.

games.q: you're Kama, crouched behind a bush with a flower-tipped arrow. Shiva sits still under a tree, and Parvati stands near. what happens when you shoot?
o: nothing at all; Shiva never stirs.
Shiva stirs, sees you, and the third eye burns you to ash.
Shiva falls in love on the spot and marries Parvati.
games.why: the arrow stirs him for a moment, then he sees the cause. fire from the third eye burns Kama to ash. desire forced from outside can't win Shiva.

practice: Sit as still as you comfortably can, and sooner or later a want will show up: to check your phone, to eat, to be somewhere else.
Don't fight it or obey it; notice it, watch it rise and fall like spring around a still figure under a tree, and come back to the breath.
If you pray, you can say Om Namah Shivaya, or the name of God you use, each time you come back.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Purana. Today: Kama burned by the third eye, and living on as Ananga.
